title: The Ballad of High Times Magazine
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of High Times magazine, the cannabis publication founded by Thomas King Forcade (born Gary Goodson). They cover his pot-smuggling background, the underground zine scene and Underground Press Syndicate, his 1970 pie-in-the-face protest at Nixon's obscenity commission, the magazine's 1974 launch and early success, Operation Green Merchant, the 1990s hip hop-driven pot boom, the Stephen Hager era, the 2000s editorial missteps, the private equity era with Adam Levin and the Cannabis Cup, the debt and receivership, and the magazine's 2024 end. The episode closes with listener mail about technicians in science.

entities.name: Nixon Presidential Commission on Obscenity and Pornography
The Long Fall of High Times

segments.title: Opening banter on High Times
segments.summary: The hosts share their memories of reading and subscribing to High Times and call it an iconic, culturally persistent magazine.

segments.title: Thomas Forcade's background and pot smuggling
segments.summary: Founder Thomas King Forcade, born Gary Goodson, is introduced as a major pot dealer who smuggled marijuana by plane, followed by his Air Guard exit, name change, and start in the underground zine scene with Orpheus, including the bullet-hole peace sign cover.

segments.title: Underground Press Syndicate
segments.summary: Forcade becomes national coordinator of the Underground Press Syndicate, a news service for underground magazines, where he learns magazine business basics.

segments.title: 1970 Nixon commission pie-in-the-face protest
segments.summary: Forcade testifies before Nixon's Presidential Commission on Obscenity and Pornography, saying censorship is the true obscenity, and pies chairman Otto Larson in the face, reportedly the first such pie protest.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: Origins of High Times
segments.summary: The magazine's origin is traced to Forcade and friends with a Playboy-style idea, intended as real journalism about activism and growing marijuana. Michael Kennedy, his attorney and later legal counsel, explains the free-speech strategy of teaching people to grow pot.

segments.title: Controlled Substances Act and marijuana policy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1970 Controlled Substances Act, marijuana's schedule one classification, and the War on Drugs as motivation for High Times' mockery of government claims.

segments.title: First issues and launch party
segments.summary: The first issue in summer 1974 had a ten thousand copy run and features like the Trans High Market quotation of drug street prices. Sales grew after a Grammercy Park Hotel launch party with brownies, nitrous and cocaine, which drew TV coverage, and the second issue sold out a fifty thousand run in four weeks with a marijuana centerfold.

segments.title: Cocaine lyric tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether the Steely Dan lyric about fine Colombian refers to pot or cocaine, with one explanation favoring pot.

segments.title: Yacht rock tangent
segments.summary: Brief conversation about the yacht rock documentary and the British spy series Black Doves, with no substantive topic.

segments.title: Early High Times journalism and influence
segments.summary: Early reporting exposed paraquat spraying of marijuana fields and helped prompt a congressional investigation. Contributors included Hunter S. Thompson, William S. Burroughs, Truman Capote, the Dalai Lama interview, and Andy Warhol. The magazine's subscribership reached roughly that of Rolling Stone by year four.

segments.title: Forcade's death and memorial
segments.summary: Forcade died by suicide in November 1978 at age 33 after previous attempts; his memorial atop the World Trade Center included friends smoking rolled joints of his ashes.

segments.title: Six Feet Under tangent
segments.summary: The hosts digress into a Six Feet Under scene about characters snorting ashes, and a joke about Claire.

segments.title: Drift into cocaine coverage and Operation Green Merchant
segments.summary: The magazine began covering cocaine and harder drugs in its price listings before returning to cannabis in the 1980s. The DEA's Operation Green Merchant targeted grow-equipment advertisers, nearly bankrupting High Times.

segments.title: 1990s revival, hip hop, and home grow
segments.summary: Under Stephen Hager, the magazine was revived in the 1990s, helped by Dr. Dre's The Chronic and hip hop culture. The magazine also taught home hydroponic growing, and the hosts link this to better marijuana potency in the early nineties.

segments.title: Stephen Hager era and NORML
segments.summary: Stephen Hager edited High Times from 1988 to 2003 and pushed for full legalization. Forcade helped bankroll NORML, and the hosts recall the Norml rallies. A 2013 The Nation article called the magazine highly influential.

segments.title: Jack Black sketch and Tenacious D cover
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the magazine's standing in popular culture, including a Saturday Night Live sketch with Jack Black as a forgetful High Times reporter, and a 2000s cover featuring Tenacious D.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: Richard Stratton, John Buffalo Mailer, and 2000s missteps
segments.summary: Richard Stratton, a former federal prisoner turned journalist, became editor in chief around 2003 and hired John Buffalo Mailer, son of Norman Mailer, as executive editor. They shifted away from weed toward culture coverage, which readers rejected. In 2005 they returned to cannabis with a Buds are back issue and Hager came back.

segments.title: Private equity, Cannabis Cup, and collapse
segments.summary: As legalization spread, private equity investor Adam Levin's group got involved. The Cannabis Cup earned most revenue, and expansion plans (casino, dispensaries, delivery, IPO) fell through, leaving about one hundred million dollars in debt, CEO turnover and receivership.

segments.title: Fire sale and the missing buyer
segments.summary: The receiver offered the brand for about seven million dollars in May of last year, and no one bought it. The hosts wish Snoop Dogg or Martha Stewart would buy it.

segments.title: Final issue and website shutdown
segments.summary: High Times published its last print issue in 2024 (last issue September 2024), and its website has not been updated since June 2024, with images broken. Pot Culture magazine's quote about the site is cited.

segments.title: Listener mail: technicians are scientists
segments.summary: Listener Rosalie Maltip writes that technicians are scientists and that the show's chemistry set episode implied otherwise. The hosts agree.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and show information.
